kurz: How investment decisions improve if you first ask what reliably loses you money and then refrain from making those mistakes.

bloecke.md:
The Königsberg mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi solved difficult problems by inverting them. If a function was unwieldy in one direction, he examined its inverse. Charlie Munger turned this into a tool for decision-making. Instead of asking how a portfolio becomes good, you ask what reliably makes it bad, and then avoid those mistakes. In his 1986 commencement speech at the Harvard School, Munger listed prescriptions for failure instead of recipes for success. The audience was meant to read them in reverse.

Inversion is more than a rewording, because it changes the kind of knowledge you need. The question of which fund will perform best over the next ten years requires a forecast about the future. For the question of what has reliably destroyed money in large samples, on the other hand, a look at the past is enough. The answers to it are stable and concrete, and you can make decisions on them today.

bloecke.quelle: Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, reported working motto (“invertere”)

bloecke.md:
## Advantages of inversion

Three reasons backed by evidence speak in favour of inversion.

First, failures are better documented than successes. Successful paths can hardly be reproduced. Of the US equity funds that were in the top quarter of their category in 2021, none of the large-, mid- and multi-cap funds was back in the top quarter in every one of the four following years up to 2025; among the small-cap funds, the figure was around 2%. Pure chance would lead you to expect 0.39% (S&P Persistence Scorecard, as of 31 December 2025). Paths to failure, by contrast, repeat themselves across decades, countries and samples.

Second, a decision on exclusion criteria can be made today. Whether a product is expensive is already stated in the key information document (KID). Whether it performs well is only known in ten years. Exclusion criteria can therefore be checked, whereas success criteria can only be hoped for.

Third, mistakes compound over time. A cost item or a behaviour gap reduces the return every year, and the deductions multiply. A single good purchase, on the other hand, only has an effect once.

bloecke.titel: Seven documented ways to lose money
zeilen: 3.4 points return difference in the following year
Disregard the purchase price when deciding
Set a cost ceiling in writing
Select by costs instead of by ranking
World weight as the starting point

bloecke.md:
The table contains the most important message of this lesson. None of the ways is unusual, and none requires bad luck or a crash. They are habits, and that is why they can be controlled.

On the first point, frequent trading, Barber and Odean analysed the accounts of 66,465 households at a US discount broker. The average household achieved 16.4% a year, the most active fifth only 11.4%. The market stood at 17.9%. Gross, that is, before costs, frequent and infrequent traders hardly differed. The frequent traders' share selection was no worse, but their implementation was more expensive. In 1999, Odean also showed that the shares bought lagged 3.31 percentage points behind those sold over the following twelve months. The swap itself therefore reduced the value of the portfolio even before any fees were incurred.

bloecke.unter: According to Barber/Odean (2000), the gap to the market grows with trading frequency, even though share selection before costs was comparable.

bloecke.md:
## How the mistakes interact

The documented ways of losing money rarely occur on their own. Investors who act procyclically usually do so with expensive products, and buyers of expensive products also switch them more often. The effects can therefore be added together in terms of order of magnitude. The result is rough, because the figures come from different samples, but it is enough to show the direction.

The European securities regulator ESMA analysed the years 2012 to 2021. Active equity funds in the EU cost 1.50% a year, non-exchange-traded index funds 0.53% and ETFs 0.31%. The net return over ten years was 9.4% a year, 10.6% for the index funds and 10.4% for the ETFs. The return gaps of 1.2 and 1.0 points are thus of the same order of magnitude as the cost gaps of 0.97 and 1.19 points. For the ten years to the end of 2025, the Morningstar study “Mind the Gap” 2026 finds an investor return of 8.7% and a fund return of 9.9%. Investors thus missed out on 1.2 points of the return of their own funds.

bloecke.titel: Fund return after three typical investor mistakes
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. The three deductions come from three different studies and do not apply exactly to anyone in this form; in order of magnitude they are realistic and halve the result.

bloecke.titel: 1.3 percentage points of extra costs over 30 years
bloecke.md:
The assumptions are €10,000, a 7% gross return and a term of 30 years. With a [[TER]] of 0.20%, 6.80% net remains, and at the end there is €71,968. With a TER of 1.50%, 5.50% remains, and at the end there is €49,840.

The difference is €22,128, or around 31% of the final wealth, excluding the initial charge and taxes. Looked at the other way round, the expensive fund must permanently generate 1.3 percentage points more gross return just to draw level, and in every one of the thirty years.

## Pre-mortem analysis

Inversion only works reliably when it has a fixed place in the decision-making process. For this purpose, the psychologist Gary Klein proposed the pre-mortem analysis (Harvard Business Review, September 2007). It is the counterpart of the post-mortem. The question of what went wrong is asked before the decision instead of afterwards, and the failure is treated as a given.

It differs from the usual risk question psychologically, but not logically. The question of how likely a setback is invites a number that you then massage in your favour. The task of assuming failure by the year 2031 and naming its reasons, on the other hand, requires a story with causes. In decision research, this so-called prospective hindsight is regarded as an effective way of finding concrete reasons. The often-cited improvement of around 30%, however, comes from a small laboratory experiment (Mitchell, Russo, Pennington 1989). It is not a reliable effect size for investing.

schritte.text: The plan, with amount, product, term and financing structure, is set down in writing but not yet implemented.
Name a specific date five to ten years ahead and assume that the result is a disaster by then. The failure is treated as having happened, not merely as possible.
Note down reasons for two to three minutes, alone and without discussion. For decisions made by two people, each writes separately; otherwise the cause named first overshadows all the others.
Write all the reasons down in a list. Evaluation and objections only follow afterwards, because otherwise the unpleasant points are dropped immediately.

schritte.titel: Adjust the plan or set warning signals
schritte.text: Each reason leads to one of three responses: change the plan, consciously bear the risk or set a measurable signal at which you make adjustments.

bloecke.md:
## Exclusion criteria instead of evaluation procedures

In practice, inversion takes the form of a list of what is out of the question. This list is drawn up before a specific offer is on the table. Its advantage lies less in particularly clever criteria than in when it is drawn up. At that point, no salesperson is sitting in the room, no price chart is in view, and the fear of missing out plays no part.

German law provides many clear points of reference for this. If a limited partner (Kommanditist) in a closed-ended investment receives distributions that are not profits, their liability revives up to the amount of their contribution (Section 172(4) HGB, Commercial Code). Capital investments outside securities law (Vermögensanlagen) carry a warning about a possible total loss in the mandatory information sheet (Section 13 VermAnlG, Capital Investment Act). Advice is available either on commission from financial investment intermediaries (Finanzanlagenvermittler) under Section 34f GewO (Trade Regulation Act) or for a fee under Section 34h GewO. Both are permitted but lead to different incentives, and incentives explain product recommendations better than arguments do.

bloecke.titel: Exclusion list from hard to soft criteria
bloecke.unter: The bottom level is never up for negotiation; towards the top, the scope for discretion grows and the share of wealth falls.

stufen.text: Individual shares, thematic funds, crypto assets up to a share set in writing in advance.
Ongoing charges above 0.5%, lock-up periods, more than two layers of costs. The written form slows down purchases.
No building up a portfolio as long as the emergency fund, liability insurance and income protection are missing or an arranged overdraft is in use.
Securities bought on credit, structures with reviving liability, products that cannot be explained in three sentences, offers made under time pressure.

bloecke.md:
The inverted question is also worth asking outside the portfolio. Asking how you could reliably ruin your own financial plan leads to three answers that are almost always the same: income stops, liquidity is lacking at the wrong moment, or a commitment can no longer be undone.

Testable rules can be derived from this. Statutory cover provides less than many assume. A full reduced earning capacity pension (Erwerbsminderungsrente) is only paid if you can work less than three hours a day, and a partial one if you can work three to under six hours (Section 43 SGB VI, Social Code Book VI). The statutory pension now only protects the occupation you trained for in the case of insured persons born before 2 January 1961 (Section 240 SGB VI). For a loan, the inverted question is not about the interest rate you get. It asks what happens with the follow-up financing when the [[fixed-rate period]] ends and an income is lost at the same time. The repayment rate and the length of the fixed-rate period depend on this question, not on the interest rate offered.

Avoiding mistakes does not in itself produce any return. If you push the inverted question far enough, you end up at zero risk and overlook the fact that not investing is also on the list of ways to lose. For a holding period of 20 years, the DAX return triangle of the Deutsches Aktieninstitut (German Equity Institute) shows 3.3% a year in the worst time window of the last 50 years, and 8.4% on average. The costs of doing nothing are less conspicuous than those of a bad purchase, but they are not smaller.

In addition, an exclusion list is only as good as its evidence. Rules such as “no shares from emerging markets” or “nothing I don't know” are not inversion. They merely supply a justification for [[home bias]]. For every exclusion criterion, you should be able to state which documented loss mechanism it guards against.

## Tax mistakes in Germany

The last way of losing money has nothing to do with markets. Losses from the sale of shares may only be offset against gains from the sale of shares (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG, Income Tax Act). Everything else, that is, funds, ETFs, bonds, interest and derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte), goes through the general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf). Investors who realise share losses in December in order to offset ETF gains achieve nothing by doing so. The loss is carried forward, and the tax on the ETF gain is due anyway. At least the former €20,000 limit for derivative transactions has gone; the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) abolished it without replacement (Section 52(28) EStG).

The second mistake is even more mundane. Without an [[Exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag)|exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag)]], the bank withholds flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) from the first cent, even though €1,000 per person and €2,000 for joint assessment would remain tax-free (Section 20(9) EStG). The tax can then be recovered through an exemption order issued retrospectively, which applies to the entire calendar year, or through the capital income annex (Anlage KAP). Both mistakes cost money, and both can be avoided in ten minutes. They do not appear in lists of investment strategies, only in the inverted list.

The forward question requires a forecast, the inverted question only a look back. The list of sure ways to lose money is therefore shorter and better documented, and decisions on it can be made today. Every investment decision is therefore better off starting with it.

mitnehmen: Inversion means first collecting the documented ways of losing money and then refraining from everything on this list; what remains forms the strategy.

Ways of losing money such as frequent trading, high costs, procyclical behaviour and cluster risks are empirically stable, ways to success are not; of the top US funds of 2021, apart from the small-cap funds, none was back in the top quarter in every one of the four following years, whereas pure chance would have produced 0.39%.
The three documented mistakes of behaviour gap, expensive product and frequent trading together cost in the order of half the return.
The pre-mortem analysis takes failure as a given and asks for the reasons, which allows it to uncover more useful risks than any probability estimate.
Exclusion criteria work because they are set before the offer arrives, but each one needs a documented loss mechanism, otherwise it is just a prejudice.

begriffe.text: Analysis before a decision that assumes the decision has already failed and asks for the causes. It produces concrete chains of causes instead of probability estimates (Gary Klein, 2007).

Difference between the return of a fund and the return of its investors that arises from the choice of when to buy and when to sell. For the ten years to the end of 2025, Morningstar puts it at around 1.2 percentage points a year.
Condition, set in advance and in writing, under which a product or a decision is rejected without further examination. It works because it is set before the specific offer arrives.

Separate offsetting category for losses from the sale of individual shares. These losses may only be offset against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG), not against income from funds, interest or derivative transactions.
